newsitem.title: USA: Congress becomes more activist on health issues.
newsitem.headline: Congress becomes more activist on health issues.

text.p: Health reform has moved from stepchild to poster child of the first Republican-led Congress in 40 years.

As one of its final acts before adjourning next week, Congress is expected to pass a bill expanding insurance for new mothers and the mentally ill and creating an entitlement for children with spina bifida born to Vietnam veterans.
The bills follow passage of a sweeping measure, signed into law by President Bill Clinton this summer, helping people keep insurance if they change jobs or have a pre-existing illness.
All this has happened under a Republican leadership that began its self-proclaimed revolution in 1995 guided by a 10-part "Contract With America" that did not even mention health care.

Further, Republicans spent much of last year pushing to reduce Medicare and Medicaid spending as part of a balanced budget plan -- only to be slapped with a presidential veto and blizzard of attack ads from Democrats and labor unions.

Health reform advocates, who watched Clinton's controversial plan for universal insurance die in a Democratic Congress in 1994, say the recent legislation was not the dramatic reform they wanted but was more than they expected.
"This is a very welcome surprise," Ron Pollack, executive director of Families, USA, said. "But we should not fool ourselves that what is being done now is earthshaking. These are very modest steps."

The turnaround is frustrating, however, for business and insurance groups that say they never expected a Republican, free-market Congress to slap them with new mandates and specify private insurance benefits.

"This is lousy policy, and it sets an awful precedent," said Paul Huard, senior vice president of the National Association of Manufacturers. "The government should not be in the business of designing health insurance plan limits or of mandating specific courses of treatment."

Both supporters and opponents of the legislation say insurance premiums could rise under the bills, although they disagree by how much. And they say the bills do not address the problem of 41 million Americans without health insurance.

Further, the rash of legislation may be coming from a Republican Congress, but none of the bills originated with the Republican leadership. Instead, most were bipartisan bills that slowly gained steam.
Analysts say the action indicates a new consensus may be forming on both sides of the aisle for limited, incremental steps to remake health care.

Democrats learned from the crashing failure of Clinton's health plan that Americans do not want too much change too fast. Republicans learned from a similar lesson from the meltdown of their balanced budget plan. Their falling poll numbers also convinced Republicans they needed the political boost that the popular health reform bills could deliver.

"Insured America is primarily concerned about itself," said Democratic pollster Celinda Lake, adding that people did not want a sweeping plan for the uninsured so much as action on costs and a guarantee that insurance would cover their needs.

Bill supporters also have raw emotion on their side, as in the case of legislation to be voted on next week requiring insurers to let new mothers stay in the hospital for 48 hours after a normal delivery and 96 hours after a Caesarean.

The measure is a direct result of accounts by mothers who were discharged quickly from the hospital, only to find later that their infant had a serious illness that might have been detected with a longer stay.
"We did not want to be branded against 48 hours and therefore it passed," a House Republican aide said.

Legislation on mental illness sponsored by Sen. Pete Domenici, R-N.M., and Sen. Paul Wellstone, D-Minn., has a similar background. The bill would bar insurers from setting lower annual and lifetime payment limits for mental health than they provide for physical ailments.

For example, some insurers now set a $1 million lifetime limit on coverage for physical illness but allow only $50,000 for mental illness, meaning that one major hospitalization may exhaust a family's insurance.
